H there,
I was looking through the TODO items on the physlib website and I got interested in the CoplanarDoublePendulum File, which has a good docstring but no results yet (github)
I started by defining a structure for the pendulum:

structure CoplanarDoublePendulum where
  l₁ : LengthUnit
  l₂ : LengthUnit
  m₁ : MassUnit
  m₂ : MassUnit
  g : NNReal

Is this idiomatic design? Should MassUnit and LengthUnit be used or should I just use (positive) Real numbers?

Now I am a bit stuck on how to define the configuration space. I see several options:

  • ℝ × ℝ or (Fin 2) -> ℝ × ℝ: Pro: Easy to acess values, con: No structure that specifies that we are talking about angles.
  • Circle × Cirlce or Real.Angle × Real.Angle: Pro: Correct structure, con: pain to work with

When this definition is done, I would continue somewhat like this:

/-- The configuration space of the coplaner double pendulum. -/
abbrev ConfigurationSpace := (Fin 2) → ℝ
variable  (P : CoplanarDoublePendulum) (C : ConfigurationSpace)

def ConfigurationSpace.phi_1 := C 1
def ConfigurationSpace.phi_2 := C 2
scoped notation "φ₁" => ConfigurationSpace.phi_1

scoped notation "φ₂" => ConfigurationSpace.phi_2

open Time
noncomputable section
/--
The cartesian coordinates of mass `m₁`.
-/
def r₁ : ConfigurationSpace → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2) := fun C ↦
  !₂[P.l₁.val * sin (φ₁ C), -P.l₁.val * cos (φ₁ C)]

def r₂ : ConfigurationSpace → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2) := fun C ↦
  r₁ P C + !₂[P.l₂.val * sin (φ₂ C), - P.l₂.val * cos (φ₂ C)]

(I just chose one of the definitions for ConfigurationSpace, it should be replaced with the correct one).

Can you give me some feedback on this? How do I learn about idiomatic design in physlib, where should I look?

Hi @Christian Krause ! Nice! To answer your questions:

Is this idiomatic design? Should MassUnit and LengthUnit be used or should I just use (positive) Real numbers?

If you want to do it with units, I think WithDim might be more appropriate to use here, although there isn't that much API around units currently, so it would likely be a lot of work. If you can get it to work great - if not, working with Reals for now might be easier.

I would define ConfigurationSpace as a structure with fields corresponding to Real.Angle. From this it should be possible to build api (lots of little definitions and lemmas) which lets you construct an element of ConfigurationSpace from reals and get reals from it. The idea here is that with enough API the exact definition shouldn't actually matter too much. The more of these sorts of little results one writes, the easier things will be in the future.

The only other comment I would have now is that r1 and r2 should likely map down to Space 2 rather than EuclideanSpace.

Regarding the design of Physlib, the easiest is probably to take a look at existing files, or make small PRs and go through the review process. We follow the same design principles as Mathlib in terms of code style. We should, at some point, write a documentation on this, but haven't got one as of yet.

Thank you very much for your clarifiction for all my questions.
I am not soure about the defintion of ConfigurationSpace. How often would this exact Space be reused? It seems kind of redundant to build a lot of API just for the Solution to the Double Pendulum. The API for going to and from Reals is not the Problem, I am rather woried about things like having a Norm or more structure that is required for stating lemmas about the derivatives of r1 and r2.

What about something like this?

/-- The configuration space of the coplaner double pendulum. -/
abbrev ConfigurationSpace := Angle × Angle

#synth Norm ConfigurationSpace
#synth TopologicalSpace ConfigurationSpace


noncomputable def ConfigurationSpace.fromReal (φ₁ φ₂ : ℝ) : ConfigurationSpace where
  fst  := Angle.coe φ₁
  snd := Angle.coe φ₂

noncomputable section

variable  (P : CoplanarDoublePendulum) (C : ConfigurationSpace)

def ConfigurationSpace.phi_1.toReal := C.1.toReal
def ConfigurationSpace.phi_2.toReal := C.2.toReal

scoped notation "φ₁" => ConfigurationSpace.phi_1.toReal

scoped notation "φ₂" => ConfigurationSpace.phi_2.toReal


open Time
/--
The cartesian coordinates of mass `m₁`.
-/
def r₁ : ConfigurationSpace → Space 2 := fun C ↦
  ⟨![P.l₁.val * sin (φ₁ C), -P.l₁.val * cos (φ₁ C)]⟩

def r₂ : ConfigurationSpace → Space 2 := fun C ↦
  ⟨r₁ P C + ![P.l₂.val * sin (φ₂ C), - P.l₂.val * cos (φ₂ C)]⟩

I think having something like: 

structure ConfigurationSpace where
    φ₁ : Angle
    φ₂ : Angle

is going to be easier here.

I understand that with this definition, you don't get things like TopologicalSpace for free, and they have to be redefined. To do this you have to build an API which is cumbersome however:

  • Even if this API is not going to be reused directly, setting it up correctly, will set a good precedent for similar problems in the future.
  • Building an API allows you to be very explicit about the assumptions being made on the configuration space. In particular, here I don't think you are actually going to need a Norm.

Maybe it is worth thinking about the overall plan here, and what structures on ConfigurationSpace we are going to need.

  • I think at some point we will need to work in local coordinates, and this is going to rely on an IsManifold instance on ConfigurationSpace. This might actually be an argument for using Circle rather than Angle here.

Ok, this makes sense, I am going to continue like this. To clarify, I just learned about Euler-Lagrange in our theoretical physics lectures, so I know how to calculate but the underlying math is shaky at best.
From what I read online, we would also need to define the Tangent Space of the Configuration Space to work with the velocities, right? Because with the current setup, I can define the transformations and the potential, but I am stuck at the kinetic energy.

While playing around with this example, I was wondering if it would be possible to generalize this:

structure HolonomicLagrangeProblem where
  /-- Dimensions -/
  d : ℕ+
  /-- Number of particles -/
  N : ℕ+
  /-- masses -/
  m : Fin N → ℝ
  /-- Degrees of freedom -/
  S : ℕ+
  /-- Enough constraints -/
  constraints : Fin (N - S) → C((Space (d * N) × Time), ℝ)

  constraintsProp : sorry -- they are independent

  configurationSpace : (sorry : Type)-- Manifold??

  transformations : configurationSpace → Space (d * N)

  transformationsProp : sorry -- the transformations satisfy the constraints and are differentiable

  potential : Space (d * N) → ℝ

  kineticEnergy : Space (d * N) → Space (d * N) → ℝ := sorry -- default value with 1/2 * m i * (v i)^2

def L (P : HolonomicLagrangeProblem) := P.potential + P.kineticEnergy

This is a very rough sketch, but wouldn't this be enough to define the Lagrangian? Solving a general problem would then just amount to filling in all the fields and proving some lemmas that the Lagrangian is equal to some simplified equation.
As I said, I am a complete beginner, so this is probably very naive... but is something like this generally possible?

In a fully geometric approach - yes, you need the tangent space, and derivatives would need to be taken with docs#mfderiv or similar (and then for things like acceleration you will need to go to things like jet bundles).

However, it might be possible to just work locally. I.e. define a manifold structure on ConfigurationSpace, and then at each point x : ConfigurationSpace you get a chosen local chart, which you can use instead of working with the whole manifold ConfigurationSpace.

We currently have variational calculus in the local setting only, and but at some point we should define it for global manifolds by gluing. (cc. @Tomas Skrivan )

Your HolonomicLagrangeProblem might work! One possible way of doing this in a geometric approach is to use to use what are called fibered submanifolds to describe the constraints. The nice thing about this is that generalise to non-holonomic constraints. (To give a completely bias reference, section 3.1 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.08923)
BTW the word transformations is new to me in this context. Do you have a general definition for the concept?

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

BTW the word transformations is new to me in this context. Do you have a general definition for the concept?

In our lecture, we called the maps from the generalized coordiantes q_1, ... q_S to the real coordantes r_i(q_1,...,q_s) transformations
I'll certainly look into your paper and I'll try to get a general understanding of manifolds to implement your suggestion above.

Christian Krause said:

I'll certainly look into your paper and I'll try to get a general understanding of manifolds to implement your suggestion above.

I think the best strategy might be to get the pendulum done, to present a really good example, before generalizing. And likely much better references then my paper :).

I am trying to define a Manifold instance for the ConfigurationSpace structure. For this, the ConfigurationSpace needs to be a TopologicalSpace. I think, it is easier to make it a Metric Space and get the TopologicalSpace for free instead of defining it directly.
But I am not sure what kind of metric I should use:

noncomputable instance : MetricSpace ConfigurationSpace where
  dist x y := max (dist x.φ₁ y.φ₁) (dist x.φ₂ y.φ₂)

Would this work out? Or do we need to take the shape of the torus into account?

As the next step for the Manifold, I have to define a ChartedSpace (Space 2) ConfigurationSpace instance (is Space 2 sensible here or should I use euclidean space?).
I started defining the first map of the atlas and it seems like a lot of work. Are there any shortcuts that make this simpler/reuse existing parts of the library?

part of the cartedSpace instance

I think I have a solution for the TopologicalSpace issue, I can just define a function from Circle × Circle to ConfigurationSpace and carry over the TopologicalSpace from Circle × Circle using TopologicalSpace.coinduced

def prodToConfigurationSpace (p : Circle × Circle) : ConfigurationSpace := ⟨p.1, p.2⟩

noncomputable instance : TopologicalSpace ConfigurationSpace :=
  .coinduced prodToConfigurationSpace inferInstance

Perhaps it is even more elegant to use Equiv.topologicalSpace like so:

def prodEquivConfigurationSpace : Circle × Circle ≃ ConfigurationSpace where
  toFun p := ⟨p.1, p.2⟩
  invFun c := ⟨c.φ₁, c.φ₂⟩

noncomputable instance : TopologicalSpace ConfigurationSpace :=
  prodEquivConfigurationSpace.symm.topologicalSpace
Sorry - on a train with bad internet. But I think this solution using prodEquivConfigurationSpace is the right one to follow. You may be able to get an instance of IsManifold in a similar way.

Quick look shows that there isn't a natural pull-back for manifold structures defined in Mathlib, though I think this should be easy to implement (maybe take a look at the Configuration Space for the Harmonic oscillator)

I took some time to learn a bit about Manifolds and I finally managed to define the pull-back for a manifold structure along a diffeomorphism (here: #40202)! The Configuration Space now has a Manifold instance, because it is Diffeomorph to Circle x Circle which gets the product manifold instance from Circle.

/--
The cartesian coordinates of mass `m₁`.
-/
def r₁ : ConfigurationSpace → Space 2 := fun C ↦
  ⟨![P.l₁.val * sin (φ₁ C), -P.l₁.val * cos (φ₁ C)]⟩

def r₂ : ConfigurationSpace → Space 2 := fun C ↦
  ⟨r₁ P C + ![P.l₂.val * sin (φ₂ C), - P.l₂.val * cos (φ₂ C)]⟩

/-- Wahrscheinlich nicht die Time derivative of r₂ -/
--def r₂_dot := mfderiv ((𝓡 1).prod (𝓡 1)) (Space.manifoldStructure 2) (r₂ P)

def V₁ : ConfigurationSpace → ℝ := fun C ↦
  P.m₁.val * P.g * (r₁ P C 0)

def T₁ (x : ConfigurationSpace) (v : TangentSpace ((𝓡 1).prod (𝓡 1)) x) : ℝ :=
  1/2 * P.m₁.val * P.l₁.val^2 * (v.1 0 ^ 2)

/-- The kinetic Energy in Euclidean Space -/
def kineticEnergy (m : ℝ) (x : Space 2) (v : TangentSpace (Space.manifoldStructure 2) x) : ℝ :=
  1/2 * m * ((v.1 0)^2 + (v.1 1)^2)

lemma mfderiv_r₁_eq (c : ConfigurationSpace) :
    mfderiv ((𝓡 1).prod (𝓡 1)) (Space.manifoldStructure 2) (r₁ P) c = sorry := by
  sorry

notation "Mₛ" => Space.manifoldStructure 2
notation "Mᵣ" => modelWithCornersSelf ℝ ℝ
/--
Let q : t -> (q_1, q_2) be a trajectory.
The kinetic Energy of the
-/
lemma T₁_eq_kineticEnergy (q : TimeMan → ConfigurationSpace) (t : TimeMan) :
    T₁ P (q t) (mfderiv Mᵣ ((𝓡 1).prod (𝓡 1)) q t t.val) =
      kineticEnergy P.m₁.val (r₁ P (q t)) (mfderiv Mᵣ Mₛ ((r₁ P) ∘ q) t t.val) := by

I manged to write down the transformations from the configuration space to the real world and also the kinetic and potential energy (of the first mass for now). I think the next sensible step would be to prove that the T_1 Term is the same as the kinetic energy in the real world for an arbitrary trajectory. But I have no real idea how i can compute these mfderivs. How can I even prove that r_1 is differentiable?

There is this TODO item which might affect you here. Basically I don't think Space.manifoldStructure is the right way to define the manifold structure on Space. Rather it needs an IsManifold instance.

In terms of these mfderivs, I think working out what the corresponding value of docs#writtenInExtChartAt is for these functions.
Thanks, writtenInExtChartAt definitely looks helpful. I will certainly take a look at this TODO item!
I created a new draft PR with the IsManifoldinstance for Space d, but I'll still have to look at the existing uses of manifoldStructure to convert them to the new system.
Great! This looks like what I would expect.
I have commented in #40202 with a proposal for a better lemma about diffeomorphisms.

I created a new draft pr (here) with the IsManifold instance using the new lemmas from #40202. The Manifold instance works fine but I'm currently stuck at proving that the Diffeomorphism between Space d (with respect to (𝓡 d)) and Space d (with respect to 𝓘(ℝ, Space d)) is actually differentiable.

The difficulty is that I have a goal which looks like this:

     ⊢ ContMDiff (modelWithCornersSelf Real (EuclideanSpace Real (Fin d))) (modelWithCornersSelf Real (Space d)) Top.top
  fun p => p

Where there are two different modelWithCorners.
With some rearranging, I get to this:

ContDiffOn ℝ ω (↑(chartAt (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)) x).symm) (chartAt (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)) x).target

where I need to prove that the inverse of a Chart is differentiable. This doesn't seem to hard but I can't find any lemmas to go further from here.
I would be glad if you could give me some advice on how to prove this or if is possible to avoid this completely by not relying on it later in Physlib?
Why do we need this diffeomorphism? I.e. do we actually ever need to use modelWithCornersSelf Real (Space d) here.
Sorry - my bad, you do need this. I wonder if it is easier to define two diffeomorphisms between Space d an EuclideanSpace and then compose them.

So if you define the manifold structure on Space d like this: 

noncomputable instance (d : ℕ) : ChartedSpace (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)) (Space d) :=
    (homEuclideanSpaceSpace d).symm.toOpenPartialHomeomorph.singletonChartedSpace (by simp)

instance (d : ℕ) : IsManifold (𝓡 d) ⊤ (Space d) :=
  (homEuclideanSpaceSpace d).symm.toOpenPartialHomeomorph.isManifold_singleton (by simp)

lemma chartAt_eq (d : ℕ) (p : Space d) :
    chartAt (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)) p = (homEuclideanSpaceSpace d).symm.toOpenPartialHomeomorph :=
  rfl

the proof you are wanting becomes somewhat trivial: 

noncomputable def modelDiffeo {d} : Diffeomorph (𝓡 d) 𝓘(ℝ, Space d) (Space d) (Space d) ⊤ where
  toFun p := p
  invFun p := p
  left_inv _ := rfl
  right_inv _ := rfl
  contMDiff_toFun := by
    simp
    refine contMDiff_iff.mpr ⟨continuous_id', fun x y => ?_⟩
    simp [← Function.id_def, homEuclideanSpaceSpace]
    fun_prop
  contMDiff_invFun := by
    apply contMDiff_iff.mpr
    constructor
    · simp
      fun_prop
    intro x y
    simp [homEuclideanSpaceSpace]
    fun_prop
Oh, thank you for this idea! Having access to the specific chart makes it a lot easier indeed.
There is also a lemma about "charts are smooth" (or perhaps "extended charts are smooth"): look at docs#contMDiffAt_extChartAt and friends
